guideTitle: 6 Best Cell Phone Signal Boosters for Home (2026)
metaDescription: Six cell phone signal boosters for home compared by coverage, carrier bands and setup, so you can match one to your outdoor signal and phone.
introParagraphs: A signal booster does one thing: it takes a weak outdoor signal, amplifies it and rebroadcasts it indoors. It cannot create a signal that is not there, which is why the first step is checking your outdoor reception before you spend anything. This guide covers six home boosters that differ in coverage claims and in how many carrier bands they support.

The spread is worth understanding. The Hiboost lists up to 4,000 square feet and the Callone+ up to 3,500, while the CELSGN lists up to 3,000 and the second HiBoost model targets 2,000. The Phonetone and GAGBK are narrower: the Phonetone covers bands 12, 13 and 17 for Verizon and AT&T at 65 dB, and the GAGBK targets Verizon Band 13 at 700 MHz.

We evaluated them based on product specs and buyer feedback, concentrating on band coverage, stated gain and how clearly each listing explains compatibility. Treat every square footage number as a maximum under ideal conditions rather than a guarantee, since coverage depends on your floor plan, construction and outdoor signal.

products.name: HiBoost Home and Office Cell Phone Signal Booster, 4,000 sq ft
products.description:
The Hiboost is the largest-coverage option here, with a listed range of 4,000 square feet. It supports all US and Canadian carriers, including AT&T and Verizon, and is marketed for homes, offices, shops and metal buildings. The listing says it supports 5G, with the caveat that it boosts the 5G that is widely deployed on existing bands.

The coverage figure is a maximum, and the honest tradeoff is that real coverage depends on your outdoor signal and building. A big claim does not mean a big result in a weak-signal area. It suits a larger home where the outdoor signal is at least usable.

Setup involves an outdoor antenna, an indoor antenna and cabling, so plan an afternoon. Keep the two antennas well separated to avoid feedback, because forced lower gain shrinks coverage. Compared with the other HiBoost model in this guide, this one targets double the area. It is the pick for larger homes.
products.bestFor: Larger homes with a usable outdoor signal
pros: Highest listed coverage in this group
Works with all US and Canadian carriers
Suits homes, offices and metal buildings
cons: Coverage claim depends on outdoor signal

products.name: HiBoost Cell Phone Booster for Home Office, 2,000 sq ft
products.description:
This HiBoost model targets 2,000 square feet and supports all US carriers, including Verizon and AT&T. It is compatible with 5G and 4G LTE and supports multiple devices at once, which matters if more than one person in the house is on a call. The listing promises fewer dropped calls and faster internet.

It is the more modest sibling of the 4,000 square foot model, and the tradeoff is coverage area. It suits a typical mid-size home or an apartment where the signal is weak indoors but fine outside.

Setup uses the same outdoor and indoor antenna approach. Keep the antennas apart, because feedback forces the booster to cut gain. Compared with the Callone+, it lists less area but is aimed at a more realistic space. It is a good fit for most single-family homes.
pros: Matched to a realistic home size
cons: Smaller coverage than the 4,000 sq ft model

products.name: Callone+ Cell Phone Booster, Up to 3,500 sq ft
products.description:
Callone+ lists eight bands: 66, 25, 2, 4, 5, 12, 13 and 17. That is the widest band list in this guide, which matters because your carrier may use bands that narrower boosters skip. The listing claims up to 3,500 square feet, though its own feature text notes that indoor coverage varies with the outdoor signal.

The detail in that text is useful: it describes coverage as depending on how many bars you have outside, with 1 to 2 bars giving a small area. That honesty is a reminder to check your outdoor signal first. The tradeoff is that more bands do not fix a missing signal.

Setup is the usual two-antenna installation. Keep them separated to avoid feedback. Compared with the CELSGN, the Callone+ adds bands 66 and 25. It suits people whose carrier uses newer bands.
products.bestFor: Carriers using a wider mix of bands
pros: Eight listed bands for wide compatibility
Listing is candid about outdoor signal limits
cons: More bands do not fix a missing outdoor signal

products.name: CELSGN Cell Phone Signal Booster, Up to 3,000 sq ft
products.description:
CELSGN is explicit about its limits. The listing asks you to confirm that your phone supports bands 2, 4, 5, 12, 13 or 17 and that you receive at least 2 bars of signal outside. It says the booster works with AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile and Straight Talk as long as those bands are used, and that it will only amplify 5G if your phone is using one of those bands.

That clarity is useful to buyers. The tradeoff is that you must do homework on bands before buying. It suits home, office and metal buildings.

Setup follows the usual two-antenna pattern. Keep them separated. Compared with the Phonetone, it covers six bands rather than three. It is a good middle choice.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want clear compatibility guidance
pros: Clear guidance on bands and signal
Suits home, office and metal buildings

products.name: Phonetone Cell Phone Signal Booster, Band 12 13 17
products.description:
Phonetone is a narrower booster aimed at Verizon and AT&T on bands 12, 13 and 17, with a listed 65 dB gain. It uses automatic gain control to detect existing signal, and it claims to improve VoLTE and 4G LTE data. The narrower focus can mean a simpler setup if your carrier matches.

Gain figures differ by source and are not a hard cap, so treat 65 dB as a spec rather than a promise. The tradeoff is that it will not help carriers or phones on other bands. It suits Verizon and AT&T customers.

Setup is the two-antenna pattern. Keep antennas apart. Compared with the Callone+, it covers three bands rather than eight. It is a targeted pick.
products.bestFor: Verizon and AT&T customers on low bands

products.name: GAGBK Verizon Cell Phone Signal Booster, Band 13
products.description:
GAGBK is narrowly aimed at Verizon and Straight Talk on Band 13 at 700 MHz. It is the most targeted pick and supports multiple users and devices. The listing promises better voice quality and fast data.

The tradeoff is that a single-band booster only helps if your phone uses Band 13. It suits Verizon customers who confirm their band first.

Setup follows the two-antenna pattern. Keep them apart. Compared with the Phonetone, it covers one band rather than three. It is a simple, targeted choice.
cons: Useless if your phone uses other bands

buyingCriteria.explanation: Use an app such as CellMapper to check your outdoor signal. A booster only amplifies existing signal. The CELSGN asks for at least 2 bars outside. With no outdoor signal, no booster helps.
Confirm which bands your carrier uses. The Callone+ lists eight bands, the CELSGN six, the Phonetone three and the GAGBK one. A mismatch means no boost. Check your phone settings.

With a strong outdoor signal, downlink output power matters more, and with a weak one, gain matters most. Gain figures differ by source, such as 65 dB for home kits. The Phonetone lists 65 dB. Do not treat one number as a hard cap.

Outside and inside antennas too close cause feedback, and the booster cuts gain. Required separation is model specific, with guidance ranging from about 25 to 60 feet. Forced lower gain shrinks coverage. Read the manual.
The Hiboost lists 4,000 sq ft and the Callone+ 3,500, but no maker can guarantee a figure. Coverage depends on floor plan and construction. Choose by realistic needs.
Look for an FCC ID and Meets Network Protection Standard wording. Consumer boosters are sold as kits with antennas and cables. Avoid listings without it.

faq.q: How do I choose a booster?
faq.a: Check your outdoor signal first, then confirm your carrier bands. A wide-band model like the Callone+ suits mixed carriers. A targeted model like the Phonetone suits one carrier.
The Callone+ lists the lowest relative cost, followed by the GAGBK and Phonetone. The 4,000 sq ft HiBoost is the premium. Spend more for large homes.

faq.q: Will a booster work with no signal?
faq.a: No. A booster only amplifies an existing outdoor signal. Check with an app such as CellMapper.
Antennas too close cause feedback and the booster cuts gain. Separation is model specific. Read the manual.
No maker can guarantee a square footage figure. Coverage depends on floor plan and signal. Treat claims as maximums.
Only on supported bands. The CELSGN says it amplifies 5G only on bands 2, 4, 5, 12, 13 or 17. Check your band.

faq.q: What certification should I look for?
faq.a: Look for an FCC ID and Meets Network Protection Standard wording. Avoid listings without it. Check the kit.
